big_idea: Changing the condition or the action changes the outcome.
learning_intention: We are learning to alter IF-THEN code and describe the effect.
student_learning_goal: I can alter IF-THEN code and describe the effect.
success_criteria: I can change a condition and predict how the outcome changes.
I can change an action and predict how the outcome changes.
I can swap branches and describe the effect.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Inspector If and Then the Action Dog — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 4 altering tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Original code: IF >10, THEN BIG. New code: IF >20, THEN BIG. What changed? Inspector If opens: 'NEW code, NEW trace!' (Class echoes.)
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Inspector If + Then the Action Dog puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we READ code. Today we ALTER it. Altering means CHANGING.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write ALTER on the chart. 'To alter is to change something on purpose. We alter code by changing a condition or an action.'

If shows two codes side by side.
ORIGINAL: IF >10, THEN BIG.
ALTERED: IF >20, THEN BIG.

'What changed? The CONDITION — from >10 to >20. The action stayed the same.'

Trace original with input 15. '15 > 10? YES → BIG.' Trace altered with same input 15. '15 > 20? NO → not BIG.' 'Same input, different outcome. The alteration CHANGED the outcome for input 15.'

More examples:
ALTER the action: IF >10, THEN BIG → IF >10, THEN HUGE. Same condition, different word.
ALTER both: IF even, THEN clap → IF odd, THEN stomp. Both branches changed.
SWAP branches: IF even, THEN clap; ELSE stomp → IF even, THEN stomp; ELSE clap. The branches are swapped.

'Inspector If says — every alteration changes the OUTCOME for some inputs. We predict how.'

'Today we alter IF-THEN code and describe the effect.'
student_actions: Listen to Inspector If alter code.

steps.instruction: Whole group: alter 4 codes together. (a) IF >10 THEN BIG → change to >5. (b) IF even THEN clap → change action to jump. (c) IF >20 THEN HIGH → swap branches with ELSE LOW. (d) IF multiple of 5 THEN star → change to multiple of 10.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Alter the code. Predict the outcome for input 15 BEFORE and AFTER.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Change Condition — pair gets 6 codes; alter the condition; predict outcomes. Station B: Change Action — pair alters the action of 6 codes; predicts outcomes. Station C: Swap Branches — pair swaps TRUE and FALSE branches of 6 codes; predicts outcomes.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: chain TWO alterations on the same code. Predict the cumulative effect.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to extending pairs: 'Stretch: alter twice in a row. Predict how the combined alteration changes outcomes.'

steps.instruction: Discuss alteration types. 'Three kinds: (1) change condition (different inputs match), (2) change action (different outcome for matching inputs), (3) swap branches (TRUE becomes FALSE behavior, vice versa).'
steps.teacher_prompt: Make a 3-column chart on the anchor: condition / action / swap. Examples in each column.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the altering tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'What did you change? How did the outcome change?' Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: INVENT-AND-COMPARE: Each pair writes TWO different alterations of the same original code that produce the SAME altered outcome for a chosen input. Two pairs share. Class explains why both work. Cite Lister (2011) trace-before-writing: alteration requires fresh tracing each time.
steps.teacher_prompt: Inspector If: 'Different alterations, same outcome. The math says: many paths to the same answer.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Alter only the condition. Use clearly different inputs.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: chain TWO alterations.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a structured frame: 'Original: ___. Altered: ___. The outcome for input ___ changed from ___ to ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Act out the original and altered behaviours. Compare side by side.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: alters the code; predicts the new outcome; describes the difference.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the altering tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: What 3 kinds of alterations did we try?
Can an alteration leave the outcome the same? Give an example.
consolidation.exit_routine: Inspector If's Day-4 refrain — class chants: 'NEW code, NEW trace!' (3x). Then carry-over: 'CHECK the IF — THEN do the THEN!' Each child writes ONE alteration they made and the input where it changed the outcome.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Code alteration accuracy and outcome prediction.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures C3.2 mastery for altering conditional code. Children at L4 alter code in 3 ways and predict each new outcome.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child alters the code but predicts the same outcome — repairing the alteration-doesn't-matter trap
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
When children alter existing IF-THEN code (Day 4 task: change the THEN action, swap branches, or add a condition), the dominant Grade-2 trap is keeping the OLD trace in mind — child predicts the post-alteration output as if the code hadn't changed. Lister (2011, 'Concrete and Other Neo-Piagetian Forms of Reasoning in the Novice Programmer') frames this as the trace-before-writing principle: each alteration demands a fresh mental trace.

Lesson 2 wrote IF-THEN code; Lesson 3 traced it; today's alteration work primes Lesson 5's capstone where children design + alter their own multi-step projects.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Original: IF >10 THEN BIG; ELSE SMALL. Altered: IF >20 THEN BIG; ELSE SMALL. Input 15. Child predicts BIG.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You altered the condition from >10 to >20. Now let's TRACE the altered code with input 15.'

The child re-traces. 'Is 15 > 20? Pause.' 'No.' 'Right. So the condition is FALSE. The ELSE action runs. Outcome: SMALL.'

'See? The alteration CHANGED the outcome for input 15. From BIG (when the threshold was 10) to SMALL (when the threshold is 20).'

Generalise. 'Inspector If says — every alteration must be RE-TRACED. The new code is a NEW code. Don't carry over the old outcome.'

Now check. 'For which inputs did the outcome change? Inputs between 11 and 20 — they used to be BIG, now they're SMALL. Inputs ≤10 stayed SMALL. Inputs >20 stayed BIG.'

If the child STILL carries old outcomes: provide a side-by-side template. 'Original | Altered. Trace each separately.' Use it as a checklist.

Long-term recovery: every alteration task starts with a fresh re-trace. Build the re-trace reflex.
expected_student_responses: (Mid) Re-traces with prompts; identifies changed inputs.
(Strong) Re-traces independently; describes which inputs changed.
(Stretched) Identifies the boundary inputs that changed; predicts cumulative effects of multiple alterations.
common_misconceptions: Alterations don't change outcomes. (Repair: alterations usually change SOME outcomes.)
I don't need to re-trace. (Repair: every altered code needs a fresh trace.)
Same input = same outcome. (Repair: altered code can give a different outcome for the same input.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child predicts pre-alteration outcome: force a RE-TRACE — child reads each line of the NEW code aloud before predicting any output.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child alters but the gate logic doesn't change: highlight the IF clause; child re-says aloud what changed before tracing again.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child alters but cannot articulate effect: side-by-side diff — original code vs altered code; child names ONE specific input where the outcome differs.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C3.2 (alter IF-THEN code).

parts_outline.task: Alter the condition in 4 codes. Predict new outcomes for given inputs.
Alter the action in 4 codes. Predict new outcomes.
Swap branches in 2 codes. Describe the effect.
